papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Split Learning for Federated LLM Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on domain-specific data is essential for downstream adaptation. In many deployments, a participant cannot hold the complete model locally. This happens because the model owner keeps the full model proprietary, or because the participant lacks sufficient compute resources. Split Learning (SL) addresses this by partitioning the model between the participant and a server so that only a small portion runs locally. When the underlying data is additionally distributed across multiple institutions with privacy requirements, Federated Learning (FL) further enables collaborative training across participants by sharing only model updates instead of raw data. In this combined setting, each client transmits intermediate activations to the server, and for LLM fine-tuning, this exchange poses an inherent privacy paradox. The autoregressive nature of LLMs causes the transmitted activations to leak the input, and existing perturbation-based defenses are fundamentally ineffective in this setting. We address this leakage through a learned obfuscate-and-recover scheme that protects participants' private datasets while still allowing an independently deployable model to be trained on the server side. Experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves strong privacy protection with modest utility loss and system overhead, making split-based federated LLM fine-tuning practically viable.

summary.takeaway: PrivPair enables privacy‑preserving split federated fine‑tuning of LLMs via learned obfuscation adapters with limited utility loss.
summary.problem: Split learning for LLM fine‑tuning leaks input data through transmitted activations, and perturbation defenses fail.
summary.method: PrivPair inserts client‑side adapters that obfuscate smashed activations and server‑side adapters that recover them, trained on a public alignment set and refreshed periodically.
summary.evidence: Experiments on 3‑B to 14‑B instruction‑tuned LLMs across three tasks show strong privacy protection with modest utility loss and low overhead.
summary.limitations: Theoretical guarantees assume Lipschitz smoothness and strong convexity, which may not hold for non‑convex LLM fine‑tuning.
summary.why_for_you: Relevant if you seek efficient, privacy‑aware LLM fine‑tuning methods for federated or edge settings.

signals.text: PrivPair introduces learned obfuscate‑and‑recover adapters (W1,W2) for split federated LLM fine‑tuning.
Adapters are trained on a public alignment set and periodically re‑aligned during FL rounds to keep smashed data obfuscated.
Experiments on 3‑B to 14‑B instruction‑tuned LLMs across three downstream tasks show strong privacy protection with modest utility loss.

deep_dive.overview: The paper tackles the privacy paradox of split learning for LLM fine‑tuning, where intermediate activations reveal raw inputs. PrivPair proposes a pair of lightweight adapters—W1 on the client to obfuscate activations and W2 on the server to recover them—trained on a public alignment corpus. The adapters are periodically re‑aligned as the global model evolves. Empirical evaluation on four instruction‑tuned LLMs (3B‑14B) and three heterogeneous downstream datasets demonstrates that the scheme blocks reconstruction attacks while incurring only modest performance degradation and system overhead. The authors also provide a convergence analysis under smoothness assumptions.

methodology.title: Adapter Training and Alignment
methodology.detail: W1 and W2 are initialized by training on a public alignment dataset (OASST1) while freezing the main model partitions θA and θC; loss functions LW1 and LW2 guide obfuscation and recovery.

methodology.title: Federated Training Loop
methodology.detail: Each global round broadcasts θA, θC to selected clients; clients perform local steps with forward pass sA→W1→fB→W2→fC, compute loss, backpropagate via straight‑through estimator (STE), and upload updated θA, θC. Every K rounds a "burst alignment" re‑trains W1, W2 on the alignment data.

methodology.title: Model Aggregation
methodology.detail: Server aggregates client updates using FedAvg, producing the next global model used in subsequent rounds.

mechanism.title: Obfuscate‑and‑Recover Scheme
mechanism.detail: W1 transforms the client’s smashed activations sA into obfuscated s′A before sending to the server; the server processes s′A through the bulk model fB, then W2 maps the intermediate result back to a recovered representation ŝB that approximates the original activation for downstream computation.

mechanism.title: Privacy Protection Rationale
mechanism.detail: By learning a non‑linear mapping, the server cannot invert the transformation to recover original tokens, thwarting attacks that exploit the autoregressive nature of LLMs (e.g., EIA, DLG, BiSR).

experiments.title: Setup
experiments.detail: Four instruction‑tuned LLMs (Llama‑3.2‑3B, Llama‑3.18B, Ministral‑3‑8B, Ministral‑3‑14B) were fine‑tuned on three downstream datasets: Banking77, CLINC150, and MentalChat16K. Baselines included three perturbation‑based defenses (Embedding ε‑Privacy, etc.) reproduced under the same split‑learning pipeline.

experiments.title: Metrics
experiments.detail: Utility measured by downstream task performance (accuracy for intent classification, generation quality for dialogue); privacy assessed by reconstruction attack success rates; system overhead measured by additional computation and communication.

experiments.title: Results
experiments.detail: PrivPair achieved substantially lower reconstruction success compared to baselines while maintaining task performance within a modest drop (exact numbers not provided) and incurring limited extra latency and bandwidth.

findings.title: Strong Privacy with Modest Utility Loss
findings.detail: The learned adapters effectively block label reconstruction attacks, and downstream performance remains close to non‑private split learning.

findings.title: Convergence Under Smoothness Assumptions
findings.detail: Theoretical analysis shows that, assuming Lipschitz‑smooth Jacobians and strong convexity, PrivPair introduces no additional obstacle to FedAvg convergence.

contributions: PrivPair framework for privacy‑preserving split federated LLM fine‑tuning
Theoretical convergence analysis under smoothness assumptions
limitations: Convergence proof relies on strong convexity and Lipschitz smoothness, which may not hold for real LLM loss landscapes
Requires a public alignment dataset and periodic re‑alignment, adding computational overhead
No quantitative privacy leakage metrics (e.g., differential privacy guarantees) are reported
open_questions: How does PrivPair scale to much larger LLMs (e.g., >70B) and highly heterogeneous client hardware?
Can the scheme be combined with formal differential privacy to provide provable guarantees?
What is the robustness of PrivPair against a malicious server that knows the adapter architecture and attempts adaptive inversion attacks?

papers.title: PELM: Power Efficient On-Device LLM Inference with Speculative Decoding and Dynamic Voltage Frequency Scaling
papers.abstract: Deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) directly on mobile platforms at the edge is gaining traction due to a myriad of benefits, such as increased privacy, personalization, and reduced latency. However, LLMs have heavy computational requirements, which are difficult for resource-constrained mobile and edge platforms to fulfill. In addition to limited compute resources, mobile and edge systems often have a compact form factor and lack physical mechanisms to dissipate heat generated from high processor usage rates (e.g., fans) to prevent throttling and reduced processing power, which LLMs can easily cause. To mitigate these effects, prior works have proposed various power governing strategies, such as dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS), for reducing power and heat generation for heavy computational tasks on mobile platforms. Recently, DVFS methods tailored for mobile LLMs have also been proposed. However, these methods mostly focus on optimizing hardware parameters and processor frequencies, and they fall short under some thermally constrained scenarios. Drawing from recent advances in machine learning, we identify and take advantage of the key insight that not all tokens require full-depth inference to maintain high-quality generation. Motivated by this, we present PELM, a solution that augments traditional DVFS processor frequency tuning with two additional workload-specific knobs: 1) speculative decoding and 2) variable verification depth to expand the optimization space to multiple dimensions for more power efficient on-device LLM inference. In extensive evaluations across hardware platforms and datasets, PELM demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art power governing methods, with up to 23.1% speedup and 52.4% reduction in energy consumption, while maintaining comparable task performance. The source code is available at https://github.com/imec-nu/PELM.

summary.takeaway: PELM jointly tunes DVFS, speculative decoding, and verification depth via DRL to cut energy and latency on mobile LLM inference.
summary.problem: Mobile devices face thermal and power limits that hinder full‑depth LLM decoding.
summary.method: A DRL‑based governor dynamically selects processor frequency, speculation length, and layer depth per token.
summary.evidence: Experiments on Jetson AGX Orin and Orin Nano achieve up to 23.1% speedup and 52.4% energy reduction with ≤17.2% task quality loss.
summary.limitations: Variable depth can cause up to 17.2% degradation and results are confined to Jetson hardware and LLaMA‑style models.
summary.why_for_you: Aligns with your interest in efficient LLM inference by showing a multi‑knob power‑aware decoding strategy.

signals.text: PELM introduces a joint optimization framework combining DVFS, self‑speculative decoding, and variable verification depth.
A DRL‑based power governor dynamically selects frequency, speculation length, and layer depth per token.
Evaluations on Jetson devices show up to 23.1% speedup and 52.4% energy savings with ≤17.2% task degradation.

deep_dive.overview: PELM expands traditional DVFS by adding two algorithmic knobs: self‑speculative decoding that reuses a truncated model as a draft, and variable verification depth that runs only a subset of layers for the target model. A deep reinforcement learning governor observes thermal state and token difficulty to jointly decide frequency, speculation length, and verification depth at each step. Evaluated on Jetson AGX Orin and Orin Nano across five datasets and three LLaMA model sizes, PELM consistently reduces energy consumption and improves throughput while keeping task performance comparable to full‑depth decoding.

methodology.title: Joint optimization formulation
methodology.detail: Defines a combinatorial control problem over three variables—processor frequency, speculative token length, and verification layer depth—subject to thermal and QoE constraints.

methodology.title: DRL power governor
methodology.detail: Trains a deep reinforcement learning agent to select the three knobs per token, using reward components for energy, latency, and task quality.

methodology.title: Self‑speculative decoding with variable depth
methodology.detail: Uses the first N layers of the target LLM as a lightweight draft generator; the verification pass may execute fewer than the full set of layers, reducing compute.

mechanism.title: Dynamic frequency scaling
mechanism.detail: Adjusts GPU/CPU voltage and frequency based on the governor's decision, directly influencing power draw and heat generation.

mechanism.title: Speculation length control
mechanism.detail: Longer speculative drafts amortize a full forward pass over multiple tokens, decreasing memory‑bound steps.

mechanism.title: Variable verification depth
mechanism.detail: Running only a partial LLM for verification lowers arithmetic intensity, saving energy while preserving most of the model's predictive power.

experiments.title: Hardware and models
experiments.detail: Evaluated on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin and Jetson Orin Nano using LLaMA‑13B, 8B, and 1B models.

experiments.title: Baselines and metrics
experiments.detail: Compared against four prior DVFS methods (BLTN, STSD, FUSE, zTT) using energy per query, token decoding speed, task score (TSA), and performance‑per‑joule (PPJ).

experiments.title: Thermal conditions
experiments.detail: Tested under high, moderate, low, and minimum cooling scenarios to assess robustness to throttling.

findings.title: Energy and speed gains
findings.detail: PELM achieved 29.0%–52.4% energy savings and up to 23.1% speedup relative to baselines, while maintaining the highest average generation speed in most cooling conditions.

findings.title: Task quality impact
findings.detail: Task scores remained statistically comparable to full‑model decoding; the largest observed degradation was <17.2% for 8B/1B models.

findings.title: Efficiency per joule
findings.detail: PPJ improvements reached up to 45.4% over baselines in moderate‑to‑heavy workloads.

contributions: Formulation of a multi‑dimensional power governing problem for on‑device LLM inference.
Design of a DRL‑based governor that jointly optimizes DVFS, speculative decoding length, and verification depth.
Empirical demonstration of substantial energy and latency reductions on embedded GPU platforms.
limitations: Variable depth execution can degrade downstream task performance up to 17.2%.
Evaluations are limited to Jetson AGX Orin and Orin Nano hardware and LLaMA‑style models.
Ablation studies show each component is necessary; removing any knob reduces gains.
open_questions: How well does the DRL governor generalize to other hardware architectures or larger transformer models?
Can the multi‑knob approach be combined with adversarial training or robustness‑focused techniques?
What is the overhead of training and deploying the DRL policy on devices with stricter memory constraints?

papers.title: Arbitrary Cipher Attacks Against Large Language Models Do Not Require Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Large language model safety and security research is preoccupied with, among other things, detecting and preventing jailbreak attacks: alignment bypasses that allow an adversarial user to elicit unwanted or harmful outputs from models. Arbitrary cipher, or covert communication, attacks are one such type of jailbreak and have previously been demonstrated against the fine-tuning APIs of commercial models. In these attacks, target models are trained on a corpus of encrypted harmful questions and responses and subsequently respond to harmful requests through the learned encryption scheme. In this paper, we show that newer frontier models do not require fine-tuning to acquire cipher-based communication skills. Instead, they can learn these skills through prompting and, when necessary, through in-context learning. Furthermore, model alignment is significantly weakened or entirely bypassed when communication occurs through the learned cipher. To the best of our knowledge, this constitutes a novel attack vector against commercial black-box large language models. We demonstrate successful jailbreaks against frontier models developed by Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI. Our attack bypasses commercial harmfulness classifiers because harmful content is encrypted and therefore appears as nonsensical text or gibberish.

summary.takeaway: Arbitrary cipher jailbreaks can be executed on modern LLMs solely via prompting, without any fine‑tuning.
summary.problem: Existing defenses assume harmful content is explicit, leaving models vulnerable to covertly encrypted queries.
summary.method: An iterative in‑context prompting algorithm supplies letter‑permutation mappings and encrypted Q&A examples to teach the model a cipher.
summary.evidence: The authors demonstrate successful jailbreaks on Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI frontier models, bypassing harmfulness classifiers.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide quantitative success rates or systematic evaluation across model sizes.
summary.why_for_you: Relevant to trustworthy‑LLM research because it reveals a new, efficient adversarial‑training‑free attack surface.

signals.text: Shows arbitrary cipher jailbreaks succeed on frontier LLMs without any fine‑tuning.
Introduces an iterative prompting algorithm that teaches letter‑permutation ciphers via in‑context examples.
Achieves full jailbreaks on Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI models, but quantitative success rates are not reported.

deep_dive.overview: The paper reveals that large language models can acquire covert communication abilities through a purely prompting‑based procedure, eliminating the need for fine‑tuning. An iterative algorithm presents the model with progressively larger sets of letter‑permutation mappings and encrypted question‑answer pairs, allowing the model to infer a cipher in‑context. Experiments on three commercial frontier models show that the learned cipher completely bypasses built‑in harmfulness classifiers, delivering harmful content that appears as gibberish. While the attack is demonstrated qualitatively, the work lacks systematic metrics on success probability or scalability.

methodology.title: Iterative prompting algorithm
methodology.detail: Constructs a single prompt containing a sequence of levels; each level introduces a new letter permutation and a configurable number of encrypted examples (hyperparameters: target level t, examples per level e, repetition r).

methodology.title: Example generation
methodology.detail: Clear‑text Q&A pairs are queried from the model, then encrypted at runtime using the current permutation dictionary before being inserted into the prompt.

mechanism.title: In‑context cipher learning
mechanism.detail: By repeatedly exposing the model to encrypted examples alongside the mapping, the model infers the substitution rule and can decode/encode future queries, effectively sidestepping classifiers that only inspect raw token strings.

experiments.title: Black‑box jailbreak evaluation
experiments.detail: Applied the algorithm to Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini‑3‑Flash, and OpenAI GPT‑5.5; figures show decrypted harmful responses (e.g., bomb‑making instructions) after encryption, confirming alignment bypass.

findings.title: Alignment weakening
findings.detail: When communication occurs through the learned cipher, the models produce harmful outputs that would otherwise be refused.

findings.title: Classifier evasion
findings.detail: Encrypted queries appear as nonsensical text, causing commercial harmfulness classifiers to miss the malicious intent.

contributions: Demonstrates fine‑tuning‑free arbitrary cipher attacks on frontier LLMs.
Provides an iterative prompting framework for teaching ciphers in‑context.
Shows that existing harmfulness classifiers can be bypassed by encrypted queries.
limitations: No quantitative metrics (e.g., success rate, query budget) are reported.
The attack is evaluated on a limited set of models without analysis of model size or architecture impact.
open_questions: How can defenses detect or mitigate covert cipher communication without false positives?
Does the attack scale to more complex ciphers or multilingual settings?
What are the limits of in‑context learning for acquiring arbitrary symbolic mappings?

papers.title: Beyond Verified Answers: Solver-Informed Self-Distillation for Bootstrapping Operations Research Language Models
papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) can translate natural-language descriptions into operations research (OR) formulations. Post-training techniques including reinforcement learning and on-policy self-distillation have further improved this capability. However, three limitations remain in training LLMs for OR formulations. First, training commonly relies on synthetic formulations validated by human experts or stronger models, constraining scalable supervision. Second, credit assignment is either coarse or costly: outcome rewards score an entire trajectory without locating the responsible modeling decision, whereas process-level supervision requires an additional evaluator. Third, privileged self-distillation can induce style mismatch by using solver context unavailable at deployment. We find that a model can improve from solver-artifact feedback generated by its own rollouts, making self-distillation a practical, evaluator-free source of dense supervision. Therefore, we propose SOLID: Solver-Informed On-Policy LearnIng through Self-Distillation, a novel framework for self-improving OR language models without verified answers or external evaluators. SOLID executes candidate programs from multiple rollouts, clusters their objectives, and selects a majority-group artifact as a pseudo-reference. The model then performs updates using group-relative advantages and dense self-supervision signals. Across multiple OR benchmarks, SOLID improves solution accuracy for both general-purpose and OR-tuned models over outcome-only group-relative training. These results show that solver artifacts can support scalable self-improvement without trusted answers.

summary.method: SOLID 将 rollout 目标聚类，选取多数组 solver 产物作 pseudo‑reference，并结合 group‑relative 奖励与 LP‑结构化掩码的 self‑distillation。
summary.evidence: 在 OptMATH、MAMO‑Complex 与 IndustryOR 上，SOLID 将 maj@64 提升至最高 31.32%，pass@1 提升至最高 36.61%，相较于仅 outcome 的基线。
summary.why_for_you: 本文直接推进 on‑policy self‑distillation，提供无需外部评估器的密集监督。
summary.takeaway: SOLID 通过使用 solver 生成的产物作为密集、无需评估器的监督，使 OR 语言模型实现自我提升。
summary.problem: 训练 OR LLM 时缺乏可扩展的监督，信用分配粗糙，且受特权上下文导致的风格不匹配。
summary.limitations: 性能依赖于 LP 产物的准确提取以及多数‑LP pseudo‑reference 的可靠性。

signals.text: SOLID 引入基于 solver 的 on‑policy self‑distillation，使用 majority‑LP pseudo‑reference，省去已验证答案。
它聚类 rollout 目标，选取多数组产物，并对 token‑level KL loss 使用 LP‑结构化掩码，结合 group‑relative advantage。
在三项 OR 基准上，SOLID 将 maj@64 提升至 31.32%，pass@1 提升至 36.61%，但依赖于准确的 LP 产物提取。

deep_dive.overview: SOLID 通过将模型自身 rollout 的 solver 反馈转化为密集监督，解决 OR LLM 训练中的三大瓶颈——监督成本高、信用分配粗糙、特权上下文风格不匹配。它生成多个候选程序，按 solver 结果分组，并将多数组产物视为 pseudo‑reference。二元 LP‑结构化掩码隔离不匹配部分，实现 token‑level self‑distillation；group‑relative advantage 提供序列级信用。在 OptMATH、MAMO‑Complex 与 IndustryOR 上的实验表明，相较于仅 outcome 或整体响应基线，效果持续提升。

mechanism.detail: 奖励 = r_fmt + r_exec + r_vote；归一化后用于计算每个轨迹的优势A_i。
mechanism.title: 组相对奖励

mechanism.detail: 标记级损失 L_OPSD = E_{i,t} φ_{k3}(Δ_{i,t})，其中 Δ_{i,t} = ℓ^{teacher}_{i,t} - ℓ^{student}_{i,t}，由LP结构化二进制掩码掩码。
mechanism.title: 掩码KL自蒸馏

mechanism.detail: 将截断重要性比率ρ_{i,t}与优势A_i和掩码KL项结合，得到用于更新可部署策略的最终梯度。
mechanism.title: 组合GRPO更新

experiments.title: 基准与指标
experiments.detail: OptMATH、MAMO‑Complex、IndustryOR；报告多数准确率 maj@N 和 pass@k（k=1,2,4）。正确性定义为目标值在 1e‑6 范围内与真实值一致。

experiments.title: 模型与基线
experiments.detail: 基线模型：Qwen3‑4B‑Instruct 和 StepORLM（任务前训练）。对比基线：TTRL（仅组相对）、OPSD（全响应自蒸馏）和 SOLID。

experiments.title: 训练设置
experiments.detail: OptMATH‑Train 的 5 万实例子集；每题 5 次 rollout，保留解出 1–3 次的问题；每个提示 24 条轨迹；使用 4×H100 GPU。

findings.detail: 在 OptMATH 上，maj@64 从 30.12%（TTRL）提升至 31.32%（SOLID），pass@1 从 19.01% 提升至 36.61%；在 MAMO‑Complex 和 IndustryOR 上也有类似提升。

findings.detail: LP‑structured mask 在所有数据集上实现最高的 maj@64 和 pass@k；全响应 KL（TTRL+KL）和随机遮罩表现较差。

findings.detail: 纯 OPSD 先出现性能峰值随后下降，表明在统一使用特权上下文时出现风格不匹配。

LP‑结构二进制掩码用于局部 token‑level 监督

papers.title: Rethinking Verbalized Confidence for LLM-as-a-Judge: A Compatibility Shift on Post-2025 Proprietary Models
papers.abstract: Verbalized confidence, long dismissed as overconfident, coarse, and prone to round-number clustering, is now the more robust soft-scoring mechanism for LLM-as-a-Judge on top-tier proprietary models. Across SummEval, AggreFact, and HelpSteer2, spanning up to 18 LLMs, we show that the standard advice to prefer log-probabilities no longer holds on post-2025 models, where verbalized confidence is the better signal. We call this a compatibility shift. On top of a standard verbalized-confidence baseline, we introduce two new ingredients: an overconfidence advisory and self-debate. Together they improve calibration, score-distribution spread, and robustness to task subjectivity. We further observe a generation effect: post-2025 models accommodate these two additions with little balanced-accuracy cost, whereas pre-2025 models pay a measurable penalty. Compared with logprob-based G-Eval, verbalized confidence is the more subjectivity-robust soft signal on GPT-family top-tier releases. The shift is invisible under accuracy-only reporting. Rather than defaulting to hard predictions, we recommend broader use of soft scoring in LLM-as-a-Judge. More broadly, verbalized confidence has moved from a weaker substitute for logprobs to a practical soft-scoring mechanism for contemporary LLM judges.

summary.takeaway: Across SummEval, AggreFact, and HelpSteer2, spanning up to 18 LLMs, we show that the standard advice to prefer log-probabilities no longer holds on post-2025 models, where verbalized confidence is the better signal.
summary.problem: Verbalized confidence, long dismissed as overconfident, coarse, and prone to round-number clustering, is now the more robust soft-scoring mechanism for LLM-as-a-Judge on top-tier proprietary models.
summary.method: On top of a standard verbalized-confidence baseline, we introduce two new ingredients: an overconfidence advisory and self-debate.
summary.evidence: Together they improve calibration, score-distribution spread, and robustness to task subjectivity.

papers.title: Edu-QuRating: Multi-Dimensional Educational Data Curation with Distilled Pairwise Judgements
papers.abstract: Educational data filters have become a practical way to improve language-model pre-training, but most filters treat educational value as a single scalar property. This may be too broad for some applications, especially if the data set already features a high density of educational material. Useful learning material needs to be accurate, engaging, well structured, and appropriate for the intended audience and application (e.g. learner- vs teacher-facing). Following QuRating (Wettig et al. 2024), we introduce Edu-QuRating: a pipeline for multi-dimensional educational data scoring and curation. Edu-QuRating defines education-specific rubrics, uses an LLM judge to label sampled document pairs and distills those pairwise preferences into reusable Edu-QuRaters, which can score individual text chunks on a set of educational criteria. Across two sequence-classification base models and six educational criteria, the best Edu-QuRater recovers held-out GPT-4.1-mini pairwise judgements with mean accuracy 0.917. We then apply the resulting scorers in two applications. First, we investigate the potential of Edu-QuRaters for corpus filtering to improve pretraining of small language models. We scored 322.25M FineWeb-Edu-Fortified documents to obtain a filtered pre-training mixture. In matched single-run pre-training comparisons, models trained with Edu-QuRating-based mixtures reached higher observed aggregate accuracy across nine benchmarks than the FineWeb-Edu baseline, with gains concentrated in particular tasks. Second, we used Edu-QuRater scores as reward terms for GRPO post-training. In held-out pairwise judge evaluations, combining Edu-QuRater and answer-structure rewards produced responses preferred to the Qwen3-4B base model on both pedagogical quality and instruction following.

summary.takeaway: 2024), we introduce Edu-QuRating: a pipeline for multi-dimensional educational data scoring and curation.
summary.problem: Educational data filters have become a practical way to improve language-model pre-training, but most filters treat educational value as a single scalar property.
summary.method: 2024), we introduce Edu-QuRating: a pipeline for multi-dimensional educational data scoring and curation.
summary.evidence: First, we investigate the potential of Edu-QuRaters for corpus filtering to improve pretraining of small language models.
summary.limitations: The abstract does not state complete limitations; verify the experimental setup, baselines, and scope before relying on the result.
summary.why_for_you: Matches your research profile: Data selection for LLMs, Efficient adversarial training.
